# Gastroesophageal reflux in children

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Pediatric gastroenterology > Gastroesophageal reflux in children*

[Original Article Link](/library/wv0hXR)

---

## Summary

Gastroesophageal reflux (GER) is the movement of <u>stomach</u> contents into the <u>esophagus</u>; gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is troublesome symptoms and/or complications caused by GER. GER is common and often physiological in <u>infants</u>. It manifests with spitting up and/or <u>regurgitation</u> after feeding in otherwise healthy <u>infants</u> with <u>normal weight</u> gain and development and typically resolves by 12 months of age. Symptoms of <u>GERD</u> in <u>infants</u> include irritability, feeding difficulties, poor growth, <u>dysphagia</u>, and extraesophageal symptoms (e.g., respiratory symptoms, <u>wheezing</u>, <u>cough</u>). Additional clinical features in children and <u>adolescents</u> include epigastric, chest, and/or abdominal <u>pain</u>. Diagnosis is primarily clinical; diagnostic studies may be performed by a specialist to confirm the diagnosis and/or assess for an alternative diagnosis in atypical or refractory cases. Management involves lifestyle modifications (e.g., dietary modifications, upright position after meals), pharmacological treatment (e.g., <u>proton pump inhibitors</u>, <u>H<sub>2</sub> receptor antagonists</u>), and, rarely, <u>surgery</u> for refractory disease or complications.




For information on this disease in adults, see “<u>Gastroesophageal reflux disease</u>.”

---

## Etiology

### <u>Transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxation</u>




GER is primarily caused by <u>transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxation</u> and movement of <u>stomach</u> contents into the <u>esophagus</u> due to: [[3]](/library/K8dUn70)




* <u>Postprandial</u> abdominal distention

* Increased intraesophageal pressure (e.g., due to large feeds, crying)

* Additional causes in <u>infants</u> [[6]](/library/Jods1I0)

* Immaturity of the esophageal sphincter mechanism in the first 6 weeks of life

* <u>Supine positioning</u>





### Risk factors for pediatric GERD [[2]](/library/68djn70)[[3]](/library/K8dUn70)[[5]](/library/58diM70)




* In <u>infants</u> and young children

* <u>Preterm birth</u>

* Anatomical abnormalities (e.g., <u>hiatal hernia</u>, <u>esophageal atresia</u>, <u>esophageal stenosis</u>, <u>tracheoesophageal fistula</u>)

* <u>CNS</u> conditions (e.g., <u>neurodevelopmental disorders</u>, <u>seizure disorder</u>)

* Chronic respiratory conditions (e.g., <u>asthma</u>, <u>cystic fibrosis</u>, <u>bronchopulmonary dysplasia</u>)

* <u>Family history</u> of <u>GERD</u>

* Exposure to <u>tobacco smoke</u>

* In older children and <u>adolescents</u>: similar to <u>risk factors for GERD in adults</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Exclusive breast milk</u> feeding is associated with a decreased risk of <u>GERD</u> in <u>infants</u>. [[3]](/library/K8dUn70)

---

## Clinical features

### GER in <u>infants</u> and children [[3]](/library/K8dUn70)[[5]](/library/58diM70)




GER is often physiological, especially in <u>infants</u>. [[5]](/library/58diM70)[[7]](/library/m8dVM70)




* Spitting up and/or <u>regurgitation</u> shortly after eating

* More pronounced with frequent and/or large-volume meals

* Normal <u>physical examination</u> findings and normal development (e.g., <u>normal weight</u> gain, no difficulty eating)

* Additional features in <u>infants</u> [[3]](/library/K8dUn70)

* Age of onset: typically < 8 weeks

* Symptoms typically resolve by 12 months of age

* Back arching when feeding

* Fussiness





### GERD in <u>infants</u> and children [[3]](/library/K8dUn70)[[5]](/library/58diM70)




<u>GERD</u> develops if <u>GER</u> causes troublesome symptoms and/or complications, e.g.:




* General

* <u>Growth faltering</u> or weight loss

* Irritability and crying

* <u>Sleep</u> disturbance

* Gastrointestinal

* Recurrent <u>vomiting</u>

* Poor appetite and/or refusal to eat

* <u>Dysphagia</u>

* Respiratory [[3]](/library/K8dUn70)

* <u>Wheezing</u>, <u>stridor</u>, <u>hoarseness</u>, choking, <u>cough</u>

* Recurrent <u>aspiration pneumonia</u> and/or <u>otitis media</u>

* <u>Apnea</u>, <u>brief resolved unexplained event</u> (in <u>infants</u>)

* Sandifer syndrome: dystonic neck posturing (<u>acquired torticollis</u>) and <u>opisthotonic</u> arching of the <u>spine</u> associated with eating  [[7]](/library/m8dVM70)[[8]](/library/Dud1t70)

* Additional features in older children and <u>adolescents</u>

* <u>Heartburn</u>, chest, epigastric, and/or abdominal <u>pain</u>  [[5]](/library/58diM70)

* Sour <u>taste</u> in mouth [[2]](/library/68djn70)

* See also “<u>Clinical features of GERD in adults</u>.”

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[3]](/library/K8dUn70)[[5]](/library/58diM70)




<u>GER</u> and <u>GERD</u> are <u>diagnosed clinically</u>.




* Obtain a comprehensive <u>medical history</u>, including:

* Age at symptom onset  [[5]](/library/58diM70)

* Feeding or eating history

* <u>Regurgitation</u> patterns

* Environmental and dietary triggers  [[3]](/library/K8dUn70)

* <u>Risk factors for pediatric GERD</u>

* No <u>red flags of pediatric GERD</u>

* <u>GER</u> in <u>infants</u>: no further management; provide reassurance.

* Pediatric <u>GERD</u>: Start <u>empiric management for pediatric GERD</u>.

* Refer to pediatric gastroenterology for diagnostic studies in case of:

* <u>Red flag features of pediatric GERD</u>

* Diagnostic uncertainty

* Symptoms refractory to empiric management





### Red flag features for pediatric GERD




The following features should prompt an evaluation for <u>complications of GERD</u> or an alternative cause of symptoms. [[3]](/library/K8dUn70)[[5]](/library/58diM70)




* General

* <u>Fever</u>

* <u>Lethargy</u>

* Excessive irritability

* Weight loss

* Gastrointestinal

* <u>Vomiting</u> that is forceful, <u>bilious</u>, or nocturnal

* <u>Gastrointestinal bleeding</u> (<u>hematemesis</u>, <u>hematochezia</u>)

* <u>Chronic diarrhea</u>

* Abdominal distension, tenderness, mass

* Additional features in <u>infants</u>:

* Symptom onset after 6 months of age

* Persistence of symptoms beyond 12 months of age

* <u>CNS</u>

* <u>Seizures</u>

* <u>Macrocephaly</u>, <u>microcephaly</u>

* <u>Signs of increased intracranial pressure</u>, e.g.:

* Rapidly increasing head circumference, bulging <u>fontanelle</u> in <u>infants</u>

* Persistent morning <u>headaches</u> and <u>vomiting</u> in older children





> [!WARNING]
> Patients with symptoms of <u>gastric outlet obstruction</u> need immediate evaluation. [[9]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[10]](/library/xd1EHf0)




### Diagnostics




Diagnostic studies are not routinely recommended to diagnose GERD in <u>infants</u> and children but may be obtained by a specialist. [[5]](/library/58diM70)




* Confirmatory studies

* <u>Esophagogastroduodenoscopy</u> (<u>EGD</u>) with or without <u>biopsy</u> to assess for: [[3]](/library/K8dUn70)[[5]](/library/58diM70)

* <u>Esophageal injury</u> and/or inflammation

* <u>Complications of GERD</u>

* Alternative causes for symptoms

* <u>Esophageal pH monitoring</u> in patients with: [[3]](/library/K8dUn70)[[5]](/library/58diM70)

* Normal <u>EGD</u> findings

* Persistent symptoms on <u>acid suppression therapy</u>

* Studies to exclude <u>differential diagnoses of pediatric GERD</u>, e.g.: [[3]](/library/K8dUn70)

* Abdominal <u>ultrasound</u> to assess for <u>hypertrophic pyloric stenosis</u>

* <u>Upper GI series</u> with <u>fluoroscopy</u> to assess for anatomical abnormalities  [[6]](/library/Jods1I0)

---

## Management

### General principles [[3]](/library/K8dUn70)[[5]](/library/58diM70)




* <u>GER</u> in <u>infants</u> is <u>self-limited</u>.

* Empiric management of pediatric GERD includes:

* Age-appropriate nonpharmacological measures in all patients

* Trial of <u>acid suppression therapy</u> if symptoms persist despite nonpharmacological therapy

* Refractory symptoms require further evaluation by a pediatric gastroenterologist.

* <u>Surgery</u> (i.e., <u>fundoplication</u>) may be considered for patients with any of the following: [[3]](/library/K8dUn70)[[5]](/library/58diM70)

* Symptoms or complications refractory to pharmacological therapy

* Need for chronic pharmacological therapy to manage symptoms

* Comorbidities that increase the risk for complications from <u>GERD</u> (e.g., <u>cystic fibrosis</u>)





### <u>Infants</u> [[3]](/library/K8dUn70)[[5]](/library/58diM70)




#### <u>GER</u> in <u>infants</u>




* Reassure caretakers that <u>GER</u> in <u>infants</u> is benign and <u>self-limited</u>.

* Consider nonpharmacological measures as for <u>GERD</u> in <u>infants</u>.





> [!WARNING]
> <u>PPIs</u> and <u>H<sub>2</sub> receptor blockers</u> are not recommended for <u>infants</u> with <u>GER</u> without <u>symptoms of GERD</u> as they are ineffective and can cause significant adverse effects. [[5]](/library/58diM70)[[11]](/library/N8d-570)




#### <u>GERD</u> in <u>infants</u>




* Encourage <u>breastfeeding</u>.   [[3]](/library/K8dUn70)

* Advise caregivers to:  ;  [[3]](/library/K8dUn70)[[5]](/library/58diM70)

* Avoid overfeeding; educate caregivers on <u>infant hunger cues</u> and <u>signs of infant satiety</u>. [[12]](/library/lAWvPL0)

* Reduce feeding volume and increase feeding frequency.

* Keep <u>infant</u> upright for 20–30 minutes after feeding.

* Avoid exposure to <u>tobacco smoke</u>.

* Consider dietary modifications.  

* Breastfed <u>infants</u>: Eliminate wheat, soy, and egg from maternal diet. [[3]](/library/K8dUn70)

* Formula-fed <u>infants</u>: Add thickening agents (e.g., rice cereal) to formula or use an antireflux formula.

* Persistent symptoms or suspected <u>cow milk protein allergy</u>  ;  [[5]](/library/58diM70)

* Breastfed <u>infants</u>: Eliminate all dairy (including casein and whey) from maternal diet for 2–4 weeks.

* Formula-fed <u>infants</u>

* Avoid all dairy.

* Consider a 2–4-week trial of extensively <u>hydrolyzed</u> or <u>amino acid</u>-based formula.   [[3]](/library/K8dUn70)

* Symptoms improve after eliminating dairy: Continue dietary modifications; discuss milk protein reintroduction.

* Refractory symptoms or symptoms persisting beyond 12 months of age

* Refer to pediatric gastroenterology for further evaluation and management.

* Consider a trial of <u>acid suppression therapy</u> (<u>off-label</u>) for 4–8 weeks in <u>infants</u> with typical <u>symptoms of GERD</u> while awaiting referral. 

* <u>PPIs</u> (preferred): e.g., <u>omeprazole</u>, <u>esomeprazole</u>

* <u>H<sub>2</sub> receptor blockers</u>: e.g., <u>famotidine</u>, <u>cimetidine</u>





### Older children and <u>adolescents</u> [[3]](/library/K8dUn70)[[5]](/library/58diM70)




#### Nonpharmacological management




Start nonpharmacological management for 2–4 weeks in all patients with typical <u>symptoms of pediatric GERD</u>. [[5]](/library/58diM70)




* Recommend lifestyle changes for weight loss (e.g., diet and exercise) for children with <u>overweight or obesity</u>.

* Avoid triggers (e.g., <u>tobacco smoke</u>, <u>caffeine</u>, <u>alcohol</u>). [[2]](/library/68djn70)

* Advise patients to:

* Avoid eating within 2 hours of bedtime

* Elevate head while sleeping and <u>sleep</u> in a <u>lateral decubitus position</u>  [[3]](/library/K8dUn70)[[5]](/library/58diM70)





#### Pharmacological management




If symptoms persist on nonpharmacological management, consider a trial of <u>acid suppression therapy</u> for 4–8 weeks.  Wean from medication if symptoms improve; refer to pediatric gastroenterology if symptoms persist.  [[5]](/library/58diM70)




* <u>PPIs</u> (preferred), e.g.: [[5]](/library/58diM70)[[13]](/library/A9dRJH0)[[14]](/library/_9d5JH0)

* <u>Lansoprazole</u> DOSAGE [[5]](/library/58diM70)

* <u>Omeprazole</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Esomeprazole</u> DOSAGE  [[5]](/library/58diM70)

* <u>H<sub>2</sub> receptor blockers</u> (if <u>PPIs</u> are unavailable or contraindicated), e.g.: [[5]](/library/58diM70)

* <u>Famotidine</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Cimetidine</u> (<u>off-label</u> in children < 12 years) DOSAGE [[5]](/library/58diM70)

* <u>Nizatidine</u> (<u>off-label</u> in children < 12 years) DOSAGE [[5]](/library/58diM70)

* Short-term use of <u>antacids</u> (e.g., <u>magnesium</u> alginate plus <u>simethicone</u>) may be considered for symptomatic relief in <u>adolescents</u>.  [[5]](/library/58diM70)

* <u>Prokinetic</u> therapy (e.g., <u>erythromycin</u>, <u>baclofen</u>) may be used in consultation with a specialist if other treatments have been unsuccessful.
